newsitem.title: USA: Houston moves to rein in topless nightclubs.
newsitem.headline: Houston moves to rein in topless nightclubs.

text.p: Topless dancers are up in arms over plans to close nearly all of Houston's topless clubs and strip dancers of jobs that have brought them fame and fortune.
Upscale topless nightclubs are as much a fixture in Houston as the oil industry and the Astrodome, and a trademark of nightlife in this sprawling Texas town.

But the Houston City Council is set to vote on Wednesday on measures that would force topless clubs out of neighborhoods, subject dancers to criminal background checks and ban "lap dances" with a rule that would keep club patrons at least three feet away from the entertainers.

Club owners said the most stringent proposal -- to double to 1,500 feet (450 metres) the distance between a topless club and nearby homes, schools and churches -- would affect all but 26 of the 119 licensed clubs in the city and effectively shut the industry down.

"It's very obvious they have their own agenda, and they are trying to ram it down everyone's throats regardless," said Bob Furey, manager of the Colorado Bar & Grill, which bills itself as the world's largest topless sports bar.

The upscale topless club in Houston is not your typical, dimly lit strip bar. The palatial clubs feature valet parking, marble floors and overstuffed chairs -- top of the line in the $4 billion a year U.S. topless industry.

Rick's Cabaret, the first topless club to trade its stock on the Nasdaq, rang up $4.5 million in sales in 1995, with some patrons paying upwards of $1,200 a year for a membership that includes access to private rooms and their private dancers.

"We are not ashamed of our jobs. We are not ignorant and we are not without any means of support besides this job. We choose to be there," said Cleo Harrington, a 27-year old dancer working on a masters degree in genetics and raising a seven-year-old daughter on earnings from her night job.

The push for tighter regulation of sexually oriented businesses was sparked by a plan to move Rick's into an upscale neighborhood near Rice University, amid growing concerns about unlicensed massage parlors and nude tanning salons that police said operate as fronts for prostitution.

Council members said the proposed ordinance would rein in the topless industry, but admit it does little to help police crack down on increased crime and prostitution stemming from the spread of unlicensed parlors and salons.

"The target of this ordinance appears to be the most visible element of the industry, which is topless clubs," Councilman Ray Driscoll said. "I don't think that is where most of the crime is going on."

Opponents say the review of sexually oriented businesses has evolved into a naked power play by conservative council members to shut the industry down, and topless dancers, waitresses and bartenders packed city council meetings last week in protest.

Janene Suckow, 25, a dancer at The Men's Club, brought her young daughter with her to testify against the proposals. "This is who you are affecting," she said. "You are taking away her trust fund, you are taking away her college education."

Troubles between Houston and its adult entertainment industry date back to 1992 when the city hosted the Republican National Convention. City officials were left red-faced when the Republican Party refused to distribute the Houston visitors' guide to delegates because of ads taken out by topless clubs.

In the years since, several other major cities have sought to rein in the adult entertainment industry. In New York's Times Square, tougher zoning laws threaten to close topless bars, sex shops and pornographic bookstores. Peep shows are giving way to more family-oriented retailers such as Virgin Records and Disney.

Detroit prosecutors formed a task force in 1995 to stop the spread of "lap dancing" where nearly naked women perform private dances at close range for big tips. Dancers call the gyrating performance an art form, but the Michigan Supreme Court said it takes topless dancing "right up to the line where prostitution begins."

In Houston, topless dancers talk of clearing thousands of dollars in tips on a good weekend. While some dancers are known to have married wealthy men they met at a club, most say working in the industry is more like "Striptease", the Demi Moore film featuring a woman forced into topless dancing to raise money to maintain custody of her child and retain her independence.
